phonemes.desc: Short alpha, smooth breathing — the name opens without roughness, like light arriving.
Pi plus acute on short omicron. The pitch peak falls on the second syllable, a rising call that carries across distance.
Lambda, long omega, nu. The long final vowel sustains and resolves the name like a held musical note.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-POL-lone' — stress the second syllable and hold the final 'o' roughly twice as long as English allows.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἀπόλλυμι (apollymi), 'to destroy, to put an end to' — the traditional Greek etymology, already proposed in antiquity, though it fits the god's plague-shooting aspect awkwardly at best

kin.label: Anatolian
kin.form: Appaliunaš, a divine name of Wilusa in a Hittite treaty of Muwatalli II with Alaksandu — the earliest near-relative of the name, pointing east rather than to an Indo-European root

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: no secure Indo-European etymology; Beekes argues for a Pre-Greek origin, and the Anatolian evidence points east rather than to the Indo-European family

pronunciation.note: Apóllōn is dual-tier because the Greek Ἀπόλλων carries both stress (acute on the second syllable) and length (omega in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Apóllōn with acute stress and Apollōn with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both are philologically legitimate.

domains.title: The Far-Shooter
domains.subtitle: Light, Music, Prophecy, and Healing
domains.lead: Apóllōn is the most Greek of the gods: not a chthonic power or a primal element, but the embodiment of measured excellence. He is the archer whose arrows strike from unseen distance, the musician whose lyre imposes order on chaos, the prophet who speaks only what Zeus permits, and the healer whose touch can lift plague as surely as his arrows bring it.

cards.name: Solar Radiance
cards.desc: The eye that sees all and the fire that nourishes; Helios is the original solar charioteer, and it is Apóllōn who is increasingly solarized from the 5th century BCE onward.

cards.name: Music and Harmony
cards.desc: His lyre, won from Hermês, orders emotion itself; music, mathematics, and cosmic proportion fall under his patronage.

cards.name: Prophetic Sight
cards.desc: At Delphoí, through the Pythia, he speaks in enigmatic verse; prophecy is not fortune-telling but the disciplined interpretation of divine will.

cards.name: Healer and Purifier
cards.desc: The same bow that sends plague can avert it; his epithets Alexikakos and Paiôn mark him as protector from evil and god of healing.

symbols.name: Laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: The transformed Daphnê, crown of poets and victors at Delphi — what he could not possess became his sacred sign

symbols.name: Lyre
symbols.meaning: Cosmic harmony and the ordering of emotion; the instrument he won from the infant Hermês in exchange for the cattle (Homeric Hymn to Hermês)

symbols.name: Bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: Far-reaching power: the plague shafts of the Iliad's first book and the unerring darts of divine justice alike

symbols.name: Tripod
symbols.meaning: The three-legged seat of the Delphic Pythia — the most politically consequential piece of furniture in the ancient world

symbols.name: Swan
symbols.meaning: The solar bird that circled Delos seven times at his birth; swans sang at his arrival and at the deaths of the greatest singers

symbols.name: Wolf
symbols.meaning: His archaic epithet Lykeios binds him to wolves and, by a play the Greeks heard, to light — the wolfish dawn

mythology.lead: Apóllōn's myths are unusually coherent because they consistently dramatize the same theme: the distance between divine perfection and mortal limitation. He is never ridiculous, but he is often terrifying — and almost always far away.

myths.title: Born on the Wandering Island
myths.text: Hera, in jealousy, had sworn that Leto would bear her children nowhere the sun shone on firm earth, and every land feared the goddess's wrath and refused the laboring Titaness. Only Delos — a floating, rootless island in the Aegean, 'the most wretched of islands' — dared accept her, on Leto's oath that Apollo's temple there would make it rich and honored beyond all islands (Homeric Hymn to Apollo 1–178; Callimachus, Hymn to Delos 18–276 embellishes). Clinging to a palm tree, Leto first bore Artemis and then, after nine days of labor, Apollo; the child sprang to maturity at once, swans circled the island seven times, and Delos, 'unwandering' ever after, became fixed to the sea floor — 'the weight of divinity anchors what chaos cannot hold.' His first act was to declare his domains: the bow, the lyre, and the unerring prophecy of Zeus's will.

myths.title: The Slayer of Pythô
myths.text: Still an infant no more than four days old, Apollo went in search of an oracular seat and found it at Delphi, where a monstrous she-dragon, Pytho — 'wondrous to behold, a bane to the crops of men' — guarded a chasm from which prophetic vapors rose. Apollo struck the beast down with a single arrow from his silver bow and took the site for his own, founding his temple above the spring of Castalia (Homeric Hymn to Apollo 214–387; the combat, with its seismic imagery of burning rock and flood, has been read as the myth of a god arriving over an older, chthonic power — possibly the site of an earlier Gaia cult). From the carcass the victor's prize took its name: Pythian. The Pythia, seated on the tripod above the chasm, spoke his answers for a thousand years. The myth encodes Delphi's claim exactly: the most sacred speech in Greece is born from killing the monster that guarded unregulated access to the gods.

myths.title: Marsyas and the Limits of Hubris
myths.text: Athena had cast away the aulos, the double pipe, because playing it distorted her face, and the satyr Marsyas of Celaenae found it. Made bold by the instrument's sweetness, he challenged Apollo himself to a contest before a jury of the Muses — terms to be set by the winner, and the story does not hide what those terms were (Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.4.2; Herodotus 7.26 passes the river of blood; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.382–400 and the fifth-century tragedians give the grisly detail). Marsyas played admirably; Apollo played the lyre upside down and demanded his rival do the same, which no pipes can do. The god won, and he exacted the wager: Marsyas was flayed alive on the tree at the source of the river that still bears his name, and his blood or tears became the stream. The myth is brutal because its logic is absolute: mortal skill may imitate divine order, but it cannot trade places with it.

myths.title: Daphnê and the Laurel
myths.text: Apollo loved the nymph Daphne, daughter of the river Peneus, and pursued her; she prayed to her father and the earth, and as the god's hand closed on her body she was transformed into a laurel tree, her feet rooting, her arms branching, her face vanishing into bark (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.452–567 is the fullest telling; the story has Greek antecedents in Parthenius and the Hellenistic tradition). Apollo made the laurel his sacred tree and wove its leaves into the crown of victors at Delphi and of poets thereafter — the Pythian Games awarded laurel long after olive oil elsewhere. Even his unrequited love became an institution. The myth turns loss into symbol with an economy the Romans admired and the Renaissance repeated endlessly: what cannot be possessed becomes the sign of achievement, and the god's failure crowns every triumph in Western culture.

myths.title: Niobe and the Arrows of the Twins
myths.text: Niobe, queen of Thebes, wife of Amphion, boasted that she was blessed beyond the goddess Leto — twelve children, six sons and six daughters, against Leto's two. Leto complained to her twins, and Apollo and Artemis answered from Mount Cithaeron with their bows: the sons died in their fields, the daughters at home, and Niobe's last girl died in her mother's arms as Niobe raised the last prayer (Homer, Iliad 24.602–617 — the story as Achilles' old father Priam invokes it, our earliest telling; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.146–312 expands). In the Iliad's version the dead are mourned nine days, buried on the tenth, and 'even then the snows of Niobe's grief did not melt' — she was turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, where a rock with a spring at its base was shown as her. Achilles tells the story to Priam to teach him that even Niobe ate after her children died. Comparative boasting against the gods is the one speech act the Greek gods never forgave.

lore.syncretism: Apóllōn was one of the most widely exported Greek gods. The Romans adopted him directly, without renaming — the only major Olympian so honored — and Augustus made him a patron of the Roman state, dedicating a splendid temple on the Palatine beside his own house. In Egypt he was identified with Horus; in Anatolia his name reaches back to Appaliunaš of Wilusa in the Hittite archives, making him one of the oldest traceable gods in the Greek pantheon. In Neoplatonism he became the principle of intellect and light; in Renaissance art, from the Apollo Belvedere onward, he embodied the ideal male form. Linguistically he survives in 'Apollo' programs, 'Apollonian' order, and the very idea of the luminous and rational.
lore.culturalLegacy: Apóllōn never stopped shaping Western culture. The Pythian Games at Delphi were one of the four great Panhellenic festivals; the Delphic maxims carved at the temple — 'Know thyself,' 'Nothing in excess' — became the syllabus of Greek moral thought. In art the Apollo Belvedere was the canonical image of male beauty for four centuries. The name flies on NASA's lunar missions, plays through centuries of music, and structures Nietzsche's pairing of the Apollonian with the Dionysian — order against ecstasy — that still frames how we talk about art. To restore Apóllōn with its full Greek accents is to restore the original sound of this civilizing force.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Apóllōn is the god who makes distance felt. His arrows come from far away; his oracle speaks in riddles; his music imposes pattern on emotion from above. He is not the warm sun but the clear, hard light that reveals every flaw. That is why he is both healer and destroyer: the same clarity that diagnoses disease also pronounces sentence.

In a digital age, Apóllōn's legacy is ambiguous. We have made machines that calculate, order, and predict with terrifying precision — Apollonian powers. Yet we have also learned that information without wisdom is a plague of arrows. The name Apóllōn, restored in Unicode, can remind us that light is not warmth, order is not kindness, and prophecy is not control.

lore.archaeology: Delphi is Apollo's great archive: successive temples above the Castalian spring, the theatre and stadium of the Pythian Games, the treasuries of Greek cities, the polygonal wall bearing inscriptions including the rescued hymns to Apollo with musical notation, and the omphalos — the 'navel' of the world. Delos preserves his birth-cult: the sanctuary of Apollo with its three temples aligned to the altar, the Terrace of the Lions facing the sacred lake, and Mycenaean traces beneath the later city — the island's sanctity reaching back to the Bronze Age. At Didyma near Miletus the colossal archaic oracular temple stood unfinished for a thousand years; at Bassae the temple of Apollo Epikourios, attributed to Ictinus, crowns the Arcadian mountains; at Amyklai outside Sparta the Hyakinthia fused Apollo's cult with the mourning of Hyacinthus. His temples framed the Greek world's most consequential questions for over a millennium.
